p1.explanation: Real. Arsenal sent dozens of used match socks to a horse and donkey sanctuary in England, where they protect the animals' legs from biting flies.
p1.con_line_false_alarm: Real. Donkeys in Arsenal socks. I have limits. Reality doesn't.

p2.tell: NPR's headline says 132 years. The magazine was published in 1894.
p2.explanation: This fake made the story less weird. The real magazine, from 1894, came back about 132 years overdue after a New Hampshire library announced a fine freeze. A believable number is still a wrong number.
p2.con_line_fooled: I knocked a century off and you relaxed. Plausible is my favorite disguise.
p2.con_line_caught: 132 years. You checked. The truth was weirder than my lie.

diff.shown: Overdue library magazine returned after 32 years
diff.original: Overdue library magazine returned after 132 years

p3.explanation: Real. In the 1950s a Nevada newspaper editor wrote a joke story about a camel race. A few years later the race really happened, and it still runs every year: fake news that came true.
p3.con_line_false_alarm: Real, and it's my origin story: a fake headline so good it came true.

p4.explanation: Word for word from NPR's New York City Marathon story: just over 2,000 runners in 1976, about 60,000 this year.
p4.con_line_false_alarm: Real. 88 women in 1976, nearly half of 60,000 now. Some numbers just grow.

p5.explanation: Real and word for word from NPR. Read all of it: she isn't saying watching makes you a pro, just that watching beats never watching.
p5.con_line_false_alarm: Real. Watching sports counts as practice now. You're welcome, couch.
